issues.legal_issue: A holograph will that is admitted to be in the testator’s handwriting and is duly attested may be proved with the strong presumption of regularity applicable to such wills, unless cogent evidence establishes unresolved suspicious circumstances.
material_facts: The testamentary proceeding sought letters of administration with a copy of the will annexed.
The will was wholly in the testatrix’s handwriting, and a beneficiary admitted that it bore her signature.

An attesting witness gave clear evidence that the testatrix signed the will in the witnesses’ presence, that the witnesses attested it in the required manner, and that the testatrix was of sound mind; that evidence was not materially challenged in cross-examination.

The will gave equal shares of the real property to the testatrix’s three daughters, and the evidence did not establish a serious illness, incapacity, or other circumstance that undermined its execution.

The trial court found due execution and attestation, sound disposing mind, and no suspicious circumstances; the Supreme Court held that the High Court had failed to give effect to the strong presumption applicable to a holograph will.
issues.conclusion: The will was duly executed and attested and was genuine; the trial court’s order granting letters of administration with the will annexed was restored.
issues.legal_principle: Under Sections 63 of the Indian Succession Act and 68 of the Indian Evidence Act, a will must be executed and attested as required by law and proved through an attesting witness, subject to the applicable rules of proof. Where a will is wholly in the testator’s handwriting, its holograph character raises a strong presumption of regularity and due execution and attestation, so that little evidence may be needed to prove it if its execution and attestation are otherwise established. If suspicious circumstances arise, the propounder must dispel them to the court’s satisfaction. The Court applied the principles in Shashikumar Banerjee v. Subodh Kumar Banerjee, H. Venkatachala Iyengar v. B.N. Thimmajamma, and Rani Purnima Debi v. Kumar Khagendra Narayan Dev, and referred to the presumption discussed in Ajit Chandra Majumdar v. Akhil Chandra Majumdar.

rule.if: testamentary_grant_proceeding and holograph_will and testator_signature_admitted and due_attestation_supported_by_credible_evidence and not unresolved_suspicious_circumstances

predicates.testamentary_grant_proceeding: A person sought a grant administering an estate under a will.
predicates.holograph_will: The will was wholly written by the testator.
predicates.testator_signature_admitted: The parties admitted that the signature on the will was the testator’s.
predicates.due_attestation_supported_by_credible_ev: An attesting witness gave credible evidence that the testator signed and the witnesses attested the will as required.
predicates.unresolved_suspicious_circumstances: Evidence established suspicious circumstances surrounding the will that the propounder had not dispelled.

issues.definition: When a testamentary grant proceeding concerns a wholly handwritten will with an admitted testator signature and credible proof of due attestation, and no suspicious circumstances remain unresolved, the will is accepted as genuine and administration is granted.

issues.legal_issue: A party alleging that a will was procured by undue influence bears the burden of proving that allegation.
material_facts: The defendants alleged that the beneficiary had exercised undue influence over the testatrix.
The beneficiary was not present when the testatrix and witnesses signed the will.
The will was in the testatrix’s handwriting and gave equal shares of the real property to her three daughters.
The evidence did not establish that the beneficiary dominated the testatrix or procured the will through undue influence.
issues.conclusion: The undue-influence allegation was not proved and did not invalidate the will.
issues.legal_principle: Under the principles stated in Shashikumar Banerjee v. Subodh Kumar Banerjee, where a caveator alleges undue influence, fraud, or coercion, the burden of proving that allegation rests on the caveator. The propounder must nevertheless satisfy the court if circumstances independently give rise to doubt about the will.

rule.if: testamentary_grant_proceeding and undue_influence_alleged and not evidence_of_undue_influence

predicates.testamentary_grant_proceeding: A person sought a grant administering an estate under a will.
predicates.undue_influence_alleged: A party opposing the will alleged that another person procured it by undue influence.
predicates.evidence_of_undue_influence: Evidence established that the alleged influencer exercised undue influence in procuring the will.

issues.definition: In a testamentary grant proceeding, when undue influence is alleged but evidence does not establish it, the allegation is rejected.

issues.legal_issue: An appellate court should not displace a trial court’s fact-based finding on a will merely by reappreciating the evidence and substituting its own impressions without identifying where the trial court went wrong.
material_facts: The trial court heard and assessed the testimony of the attesting witness and found the will duly executed and attested, the testatrix of sound disposing mind, and the will free from suspicious circumstances.

The High Court reversed that finding after reappreciating the evidence and drawing its own impressions and inferences, without giving effect to the strong presumption applicable to the holograph will.
The Supreme Court found that the trial court’s findings rested on the evidence and a proper application of the law, while the High Court’s approach relied on surmises and conjectures.
issues.conclusion: The High Court’s judgment was set aside and the trial court’s order was restored.
issues.legal_principle: An appellant must show where the judgment under appeal is wrong and cannot merely seek reassessment of the evidence. In a fact-dependent appeal, the appellate court must give appropriate weight to the trial judge’s opportunity to observe witnesses and assess credibility. The Court relied on Sarju Prasad Ramdoe Saha v. Jwaleshwari Pratap Narain Singh and Madhusudan Das v. Smt. Narayani Bai, and applied the will-proof principles in Shashikumar Banerjee v. Subodh Kumar Banerjee.

rule.if: appeal_from_testamentary_grant_order and trial_court_assessed_witnesses_firsthand and trial_finding_supported_by_evidence and appellate_court_substituted_impressions_without_identifying_error

predicates.appeal_from_testamentary_grant_order: A party appealed an order concerning a grant based on a will.
predicates.trial_court_assessed_witnesses_firsthand: The trial court heard and assessed witnesses whose testimony bore on the disputed facts.
predicates.trial_finding_supported_by_evidence: The trial court’s finding was supported by the evidence and a proper application of the law.
predicates.appellate_court_substituted_impressions_: The appellate court replaced the trial court’s assessment with its own impressions without identifying a material error in the trial court’s reasoning.

issues.definition: When an appeal from a testamentary grant order challenges a supported finding made after the trial court assessed witnesses firsthand, and the appellate court substitutes its impressions without identifying error, the appellate judgment is set aside and the trial order is restored.
